These are the lecture notes for *Monte Carlo Methods* (EN.553.433/633), a course in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics at Johns Hopkins University. The notes are loosely based on course materials by [Dr. Jim Spall](https://sites.google.com/view/james-spall/teaching) and on the textbook by Rubinstein and Kroese [@rubinstein2017].

We assume a first course in probability, in statistics and in linear algebra. You should be comfortable with expectation, variance, independence and conditional distributions, and with the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. Most importantly, you should know the theory of estimators, because every Monte Carlo method is an estimator. If any of this is rusty, the [probability review](chapters/probability-review/index.qmd) collects the facts we use most often.

These notes are driven by exercises. Most results are not stated for you to read - they are posed as questions for you to work out. You will need your answers to follow the rest of the chapter. Read these notes with pen and paper, and try each exercise before moving on, since that is where most of the learning happens!

Most chapters also have interactive apps and figures, which run the simulations in your browser. You are encouraged to experiment with them. Playing with a method is one of the best ways to build an intuition for it.

Every page has a comment thread at the bottom, which you can post to with a GitHub account. Please use it to ask a question, or to tell us about a typo or a mistake.
